author: jestfi
text:
There is a pretty wild trade developing around $PONS and $CASHCAT right now, but I think most people are looking at it the wrong way.

This isn’t simply “a whale is short, let’s squeeze him.”

Loracle has built one of the largest public bearish bets against the Robinhood Chain ecosystem, survived millions in unrealized losses, kept adding while the trade moved against him, attacked the actual Pons business model while holding the short, then watched the whole position swing back into millions of dollars of profit.

Now he’s taking money off the table while the other side is actively trying to make his exit more expensive.

The story started getting serious around September 1.

Loracle was short roughly 9.1M PONS with an average entry around $0.45 and 22.5M CASHCAT around $0.23. Both were 3x positions.

Instead of cutting when the market moved against him, he kept adding.

As PONS ran toward $1, his position eventually grew to roughly $23M. At one point he was sitting on almost $7M in unrealized losses on PONS alone, with liquidation around $1.82.

That is where this stopped being a normal short.

Most traders would either close or wait.

Loracle did something else.

While short PONS, he used Fable 5.1 to build pez family, a zero-platform-fee fork of the Pons launchpad.

Think about the incentives here.

He wasn’t only betting that the token would fall.

He was publicly attacking one of the reasons the token had value in the first place.

The bear case was basically:

Pons is not technologically defensible.
The contracts and product can be reproduced.
The fee model can be undercut.
If the launchpad loses its moat, the premium attached to $PONS should compress.

Whether https://t.co/Iz6KXtCwKO itself succeeds is almost irrelevant.

The interesting part is that a trader with a massive short was able to turn his trade thesis into a competing product.

That’s not something you see every day.

And initially, it looked like the market was going to destroy him for it.

PONS kept climbing. His losses expanded. CT started treating his liquidation price as a target. The short itself became part of the PONS narrative.

Then the market reversed.

By September 14, the same trade that had been deeply underwater had completely flipped.

Loracle still had roughly 27.47M PONS short and 35.95M CASHCAT short. The positions were worth around $14.3M and $5.7M respectively, with roughly $5.7M in combined unrealized profit.

He then started reducing both positions.

Later that day the tracked exposure had fallen to roughly 27.08M PONS and 35.44M CASHCAT.

So give him credit where it’s due:

he didn’t get squeezed.

He survived the squeeze attempt and got paid.

But this is where the second half of the trade gets much more interesting.

Because Loracle now has a problem that didn’t exist when he was building the short.

He needs an exit.

A short is future demand.

Every PONS or CASHCAT he sells short eventually has to be bought back if he wants to realize the trade.

When his remaining PONS position was around $14-15M and CASHCAT around $5-6M, fully closing both implied roughly $20M of gross buy-to-cover flow.

That doesn’t mean someone presses a $20M market-buy button.

He can reduce gradually, use limit orders, hedge elsewhere or wait for deeper liquidity.

But mechanically, the further he exits, the more his own trade changes from sell pressure into buy pressure.

And the market knows exactly where that demand is sitting because the position is public.

That’s why the next part matters.

While Loracle has been shorting PONS, the Pons protocol itself has effectively been sitting on the other side of the market through buybacks.

Over the latest seven-day period, Pons reportedly generated around $7.99M in protocol revenue and used roughly $7.02M for buybacks.

More than 31% of the original PONS supply has now been burned.

reason.inference: trader analyzing shorts vs. buybacks, neutral on near-term but monitoring Loracle position reduction
